summary.title: Can giant planets form by gravitational fragmentation of discs? Radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the inner disc region
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the feasibility of giant planet formation via gravitational fragmentation in the inner regions of protostellar discs using radiative hydrodynamic simulations. The authors employ a newly developed method to treat the energy equation and equation of state in Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations, accounting for radiative transfer effects, hydrogen chemical states, and dust properties. Two specific disc configurations are examined: one heated by a constant background radiation field of 10 K and another with additional heating from the central star. The simulations focus on the inner disc region (R < 40 AU) around a 0.5 M⊙ star with a 0.07 M⊙ disc. The results demonstrate that in the low-background heating case, the disc is gravitationally unstable at radii of 30-35 AU but fails to fragment because it cannot cool fast enough, with cooling times exceeding two orbital periods. In the stellar heating case, the disc is stabilized and does not become gravitationally unstable, preventing fragmentation entirely. These findings corroborate previous studies by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), despite differences in radiative transfer treatments. The study concludes that gravitational fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii less than 50 AU, as the necessary conditions for rapid cooling and gravitational instability are not simultaneously met in the inner disc regions. This supports the core accretion model or fragmentation at larger radii, where objects formed are more likely to be brown dwarfs or ejected rather than migrating inwards to become hot Jupiters.

claims.description: Gravitational fragmentation cannot form giant planets in the inner disc regions of solar-type stars.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the feasibility of giant planet formation via gravitational fragmentation in the inner regions of protostellar discs using radiative hydrodynamic simulations. The authors employ a newly developed method to treat the energy equation and equation of state in Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations, accounting for radiative transfer effects, hydrogen chemical states, and dust properties. Two specific disc configurations are examined: one heated by a constant background radiation field of 10 K and another with additional heating from the central star. The simulations focus on the inner disc region (R < 40 AU) around a 0.5 M⊙ star with a 0.07 M⊙ disc. The results demonstrate that in the low-background heating case, the disc is gravitationally unstable at radii of 30-35 AU but fails to fragment because it cannot cool fast enough, with cooling times exceeding two orbital periods. In the stellar heating case, the disc is stabilized and does not become gravitationally unstable, preventing fragmentation entirely. These findings corroborate previous studies by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), despite differences in radiative transfer treatments. The study concludes that gravitational fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii less than 50 AU, as the necessary conditions for rapid cooling and gravitational instability are not simultaneously met in the inner disc regions. This supports the core accretion model or fragmentation at larger radii, where objects formed are more likely to be brown dwarfs or ejected rather than migrating inwards to become hot Jupiters.

Research Context
Disc fragmentation has been proposed as a mechanism for giant planet formation at close distances. It is debatable whether this mechanism functions in the inner region of real discs. Core accretion is limited by long formation timescales compared to disc lifetimes. Gravitational fragmentation occurs on a dynamical timescale, within a few hundred years. Two conditions must be met: gravitational instability and fast cooling. Previous simulations produced contradictory results due to different radiative transfer treatments. Analytic studies suggest convection cannot provide required cooling close to the star.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to investigate the thermodynamics of discs and the probability of fragmentation. The central question is whether giant planets can form by gravitational fragmentation in the inner disc. The hypothesis is that radiative effects prevent fragmentation in the inner regions. The authors predict that discs will not fragment due to cooling or stability issues. The study tests if the new energy equation method reproduces known analytic solutions. The expected outcome is that cooling times exceed the fragmentation threshold.

Methodological Details
The simulations use the SPH code dragon with an octal tree and adaptive smoothing. The energy equation is treated with a method accounting for radiative transfer. The equation of state includes hydrogen and helium chemical states and degrees of freedom. Dust opacity is parameterized by Bell & Lin (1994), including ice and sublimation effects. The simulated disc has a mass of 0.07 M⊙ around a 0.5 M⊙ star. The disc initially extends from 2 to 40 AU. The initial surface density profile is Σ(R) ∼ R−1/2. The initial temperature profile is T(R) ∼ R−1. Two cases are simulated: constant background heating and stellar irradiation. The simulations use 2×10^5 SPH particles to represent the disc.

Procedures And Architectures
The code uses artificial viscosity with the Balsara switch and Runge-Kutta integration. The method accounts for compressional, viscous, and radiation heating and cooling. The gas is assumed to be a mixture of hydrogen and helium. The opacity changes due to ice mantle melting and dust sublimation. The disc initial thickness is calculated by balancing gravitational and pressure forces. The simulations run until the disc reaches a quasi-steady state. A smaller particle count test (5×10^4) was performed to check convergence. The vertical temperature profile is compared with analytic calculations by Hubeny (1990).

Key Results
In the 10 K background case, the disc does not fragment. The disc is Toomre unstable at radii of 30-35 AU. The cooling time is generally greater than 2 orbital periods. Weak spiral arms form but do not show tendency to fragment. In the stellar heating case, the disc is not gravitationally unstable. The Toomre parameter Q is greater than 1.5 in the stellar heating case. The disc appears axisymmetric with no signs of spiral arms in the stellar case. Temperatures in the 10 K case are ~15% higher than Boley et al. (2006). Temperatures are less than 3% higher than Cai et al. (2007). The vertical temperature profile matches the Hubeny (1990) analytic model.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets at radii less than 50 AU. The inability to cool fast enough prevents fragmentation in the inner disc. The results corroborate previous findings by Boley et al. and Cai et al. Objects formed at larger radii are likely brown dwarfs or ejected. Planetary mass objects at large radii are unlikely to migrate inwards.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study focuses only on the inner disc region (R < 40 AU). Contributions from metals are ignored in the equation of state. The simulations do not include convection explicitly. The results are specific to the chosen disc mass and stellar mass. The comparison with Boley et al. shows slight temperature differences.

Claims
Gravitational fragmentation cannot form giant planets in the inner disc regions of solar-type stars. The disc does not fragment in either simulated case. Cooling times exceed the required threshold for fragmentation. Stellar heating stabilizes the disc against instability. Some previous studies suggested convection could allow fragmentation. Core accretion or fragmentation at larger radii are more likely mechanisms. Hot Jupiters are unlikely to form via inner disc fragmentation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A convergence test with 5×10^4 particles showed essentially the same evolution. The vertical temperature profile was validated against analytic calculations. The code reproduces detailed 3D results of Masunaga & Inutsuka (2000).

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the evolution of disc internal energy for both cases. Figure 2 shows the column density and density cross-section for the 10 K case. Figure 4 shows the Toomre parameter in the x-y and x-z planes. Figure 5 shows the cooling time in units of the orbital period. Figure 8 compares the vertical temperature profile with Hubeny (1990). Figure 14 shows the Toomre parameter and cooling time for the stellar heating case.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that inner disc fragmentation is suppressed by cooling and stability constraints. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative comparison of cooling times and Toomre parameters against fragmentation criteria. 3. The future path involves investigating fragmentation at larger radii or different disc masses.
